epristeride.text: Hair-loss forum users discuss epristeride as a finasteride-like DHT blocker for keeping scalp hair. Its hair use was explored but never approved, and it is marketed in China for prostate enlargement, so the appearance use rests on its mechanism and limited data.

alfatradiol-ell-cranell-alpha.text: Users apply alfatradiol, sold in Germany and Latin America, as a non-finasteride option for pattern hair loss in men and women. It has been studied for this use in trials, which describe slowed loss with little regrowth.

topilutamide-fluridil.text: Topilutamide is a scalp antiandrogen sold in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, and users interested in topical alternatives to oral DHT blockers discuss it for pattern hair loss. It is studied for this use, though published trial data is small.

dimethylcurcumin-asc-j9.text: ASC-J9 is an experimental anti-androgen that has attracted interest as a topical acne approach because it reduces androgen receptor protein. It reached two Phase 2 acne trials, but no results were found, so the appearance benefit remains a theory.

drospirenone.text: Drospirenone-containing contraceptive pills are used by women for clearer skin because the progestin has anti-androgen activity. The FDA labels certain drospirenone pills for moderate acne in women who also want contraception, so the acne use is studied.

dienogest.text: Dienogest is a progestin in some pills that are prescribed to women partly for acne, because of its anti-androgenic profile. Its acne link rests on that pharmacology and pill-level use, with no acne-specific trials in the sources reviewed.

chlormadinone-acetate.text: Chlormadinone acetate pills, sold in parts of Europe, are used by women for acne and oily skin thanks to the progestin's anti-androgen action. Support comes from open-label studies rather than large controlled trials.

nomegestrol-acetate.text: Nomegestrol acetate is a European pill progestin with mild anti-androgenic activity, and some discussion links it to skin benefits for acne-prone users. That link is inferred from its pharmacology, and no acne trial was found.

abiraterone-acetate.text: Abiraterone is a prostate-cancer drug that lowers testosterone and DHT, so it comes up in androgen-focused discussion as a theoretical route to protecting scalp hair or skin. It is not used for appearance, and no hair or skin studies were found in the sources reviewed.

chain: Slightly less sebum or body hair
cimetidine.text: Cimetidine, an acid reducer, has been tried occasionally for acne and excess hair growth in women because of weak antiandrogen activity. References describe that effect as small, and the appearance use is a side-effect-based, off-label idea.

erythromycin-acne.text: Topical erythromycin is a prescription antibiotic labelled in the US for acne, and users typically pair it with benzoyl peroxide to limit bacterial resistance. It is studied and approved for this specific appearance use.

sulfacetamide.text: Sulfacetamide, usually combined with sulfur, is a prescription lotion or wash used for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis, giving clearer and less red skin. These uses are the product's labelled indications and are clinically studied.

nadifloxacin.text: Nadifloxacin is a topical antibiotic cream used for acne in Japan, parts of Europe and Asia, and people elsewhere discuss it as an import option. Its main use is acne, where it has been studied in clinical settings.

azithromycin-pulse-acne.text: Dermatologists sometimes prescribe short, intermittent azithromycin courses off-label for inflammatory acne, often when other options are not suitable. Evidence consists of small head-to-head trials.

aminolevulinic-acid-photodynamic-therapy.text: Clinics use ALA with light for actinic keratoses, and it is investigated for acne and skin quality, where users hope for less oil and clearer skin. The acne use is investigational, with mixed trial signals.

chain: New skin forms in its place
Smoother texture, less pigment and scarring
trichloroacetic-acid-tca-peel.text: TCA peels are done by clinicians to improve skin texture, uneven pigment and acne scars, with visible skin renewal after healing. Registered trials exist for these uses, but outcomes were not reported in the records reviewed.

corticosteroid-injection-kenalog-for-cys.text: Acne forum users describe a clinician-given triamcinolone injection as a way to shrink and calm one large inflamed pimple quickly. It is an off-label procedure, and no acne-cyst trials were found in the sources used.

basil-oil-acne.text: Basil oil is promoted in natural-skincare circles as a topical for acne because it shows antibacterial activity in the lab, including against the acne bacterium. The evidence is in vitro only, and no human acne studies were found.

seaweed-oligosaccharides.text: Seaweed oligosaccharides are marketed as a complementary topical ingredient for acne-prone skin. The support is a single literature review, which also describes a zinc complex form.

bumetanide.text: Bumetanide appears in gray-market water-pill talk among people aiming for a drier, sharper facial look. It is a prescription diuretic for edema, and no study has tested it for facial puffiness.

torsemide.text: Torsemide is mentioned in depuffing circles as a strong water pill for a leaner, more defined face. It is a prescription drug for heart-failure fluid overload and has not been studied for appearance.

hydrochlorothiazide.text: Some forum users discuss hydrochlorothiazide as a daily water pill for facial puffiness. It is a common blood-pressure drug, and the appearance use rests on anecdote with no appearance studies.

chlortalidone.text: Chlortalidone turns up in forum lists of possible water pills for a less puffy face. It is a long-acting blood-pressure diuretic, with no appearance data.

indapamide.text: Indapamide is a blood-pressure diuretic that is occasionally raised as a water-pill option for facial puffiness. It has large stroke-prevention trials behind it, but nothing on appearance or depuffing.

metolazone.text: Metolazone is a potent diuretic, usually used with loop diuretics in heart failure, and it is occasionally mentioned in water-pill discussions for a drier look. No appearance data exists.

acetazolamide-diamox.text: Acetazolamide is a diuretic used for glaucoma, edema and altitude sickness, and some users consider it for facial puffiness because it increases water excretion. Nothing shows it reduces facial puffiness.

triamterene.text: Triamterene is a potassium-sparing diuretic, mostly paired with hydrochlorothiazide, that is occasionally mentioned in water-pill discussions. No study has tested it for facial puffiness.

chain: Mild diuretic removes sodium and water
amiloride.text: Amiloride is a mild potassium-sparing diuretic used with other diuretics, and it is sometimes mentioned in water-retention talk. No research addresses facial puffiness.

eplerenone.text: Eplerenone is discussed on forums mainly as a costly spironolactone alternative for people wanting an aldosterone blocker, sometimes with water retention in mind. It is approved for heart failure and hypertension, with no appearance studies.

tolvaptan.text: Tolvaptan is a prescription drug that makes the body excrete free water, and it is occasionally raised in depuffing discussion for that reason. It is approved for hyponatremia and kidney disease, with no appearance data.
